Unit 3: National Income and Price Determination
Unit 5: Long-Run Consequences of Stabilization Policies
Unit 6: Open Economy: International Trade and Finance

terms.def: The ability to produce more of a good than another producer with the same resources, or the same amount with fewer resources.
terms.topicTitle: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade

terms.def: The graph of aggregate demand, short-run aggregate supply and long-run aggregate supply against the price level and real GDP. Short-run equilibrium is where AD meets SRAS; long-run equilibrium is where both meet on LRAS.
terms.topicTitle: Equilibrium in the Aggregate Demand-Aggregate Supply (AD-AS) Model

terms.def: The total amount of real output that households, firms, the government and foreigners plan to buy at each price level: C + I + G + (X - M). The AD curve slopes down.

A framework in which banks hold so many reserves that reserve supply sits in the flat part of reserve demand, so changing the quantity of reserves does not move the policy rate. The central bank sets the rate with administered rates. Its graph is the reserve market.

A rise in the value of a currency: one unit buys more of another currency than before. Its opposite, depreciation, is a fall in value; when one currency appreciates against another, the other depreciates.
One of the two number lines of a graph: the horizontal axis runs across the bottom and the vertical axis runs up the side. Each is labeled with the variable it measures.

The record of every transaction between a country's residents and the rest of the world over a period, such as a year. It has two parts, the current account and the capital and financial account, which sum to zero.
Exports of goods and services minus imports of goods and services: net exports. It is the largest part of the current account; a negative balance is a trade deficit.
aka: balance of trade in goods and services

terms.def: A table of what a bank owns (assets: reserves, loans, bonds) and what it owes (liabilities: deposits), with owners' equity balancing the two sides. Also called a T-account.
terms.topicTitle: Banking and the Expansion of the Money Supply

terms.def: The effect on real GDP of raising government spending and taxes by the same amount. The spending and tax multipliers add to 1, so output rises by the amount of the spending.
Comparing the crossing point before and after a curve shifts (E1 and E2), on both axes, to say which way each variable moved.
The prices of existing bonds move opposite to market interest rates. A bond pays a fixed amount, so when new bonds pay more, buyers pay less for an old one.

The amount by which a government's outlays (spending, transfer payments and interest) exceed its tax revenue in one year. Revenue above outlays is a budget surplus; revenue equal to outlays is a balanced budget.
terms.topicTitle: Government Deficits and the National Debt

terms.def: The repeated rise and fall of real GDP around its trend: an expansion (rising output) and a contraction (falling output), with a peak and a trough as the turning points. A severe, lasting contraction is a recession.

The part of the balance of payments that records purchases and sales of assets, such as bonds, stocks, real estate and firms. A foreign purchase of a domestic asset is a credit; a resident's purchase of a foreign asset is a debit.
Capital goods are made goods used to produce other goods, such as machines and factories; consumer goods are used by households. Making more capital goods today shifts the future PPC outward more.
terms.topicTitle: Opportunity Cost and the Production Possibilities Curve (PPC)

terms.def: The ordered links from a policy action to its result: for monetary policy, the tool, the policy rate, other interest rates, interest-sensitive spending, AD, then output, the price level and unemployment.
terms.topicTitle: Fiscal and Monetary Policy Actions in the Short Run

terms.def: The institution that oversees a country's banks and money. In the United States it is the Federal Reserve, which sets reserve requirements and interest rate policy.
terms.topicTitle: Banking and the Expansion of the Money Supply

terms.def: Latin for "other things equal": the rule that a curve holds every influence fixed except the two variables it graphs.
terms.topicTitle: Shifts Versus Movements Along a Curve

terms.def: A model of the economy in which households sell factors of production to firms for income and spend that income on firms' goods and services, so money and goods flow in opposite loops.
The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer. Specializing by comparative advantage is what creates gains from trade.
terms.topicTitle: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade

terms.def: Consumer price index: the cost of a basket of goods and services that typical households buy, divided by its cost in the base year, times 100.
A point on a graph written as an ordered pair (horizontal value, vertical value), such as (300, 10).
Inflation caused by short-run aggregate supply shifting left, as when input costs rise: the price level rises while real GDP falls. Rising prices with falling output is stagflation.
terms.topicTitle: Changes in the AD-AS Model in the Short Run

terms.def: The fall in private investment (and other interest-sensitive spending) that happens when government borrowing to pay for a deficit raises the demand for loanable funds and the real interest rate.

The part of the balance of payments that records the balance of trade in goods and services, net income from abroad (interest, dividends, wages) and net transfers. A negative balance is a current account deficit.
Unemployment caused by a fall in total spending and output during a downturn; it equals the actual unemployment rate minus the natural rate.
A fall in prices in general, so the inflation rate is negative. Disinflation is different: inflation slows, but prices are still rising.
A sudden change in spending at every price level that shifts AD. A positive demand shock shifts it right; a negative one shifts it left.
terms.topicTitle: Changes in the AD-AS Model in the Short Run

terms.def: Inflation caused by aggregate demand shifting right: more spending pulls up the price level while real GDP rises in the short run.
terms.topicTitle: Changes in the AD-AS Model in the Short Run

terms.def: Anything other than the price level that changes consumption, investment, government spending or net exports, such as wealth, expectations, taxes or foreign incomes. It shifts the whole AD curve.

Anything other than the good's own price that changes demand and shifts the curve: tastes, income (normal and inferior goods), the prices of substitutes and complements, expectations and the number of buyers.

Something other than the exchange rate itself that shifts the demand for or supply of a currency: tastes, relative incomes, relative price levels, relative real interest rates and expectations. Changes in policy work through them.
terms.topicTitle: Effect of Changes in Policies and Economic Conditions on the Foreign Exchange Market

terms.def: A change in production costs at a given price level, such as input prices, productivity, taxes or subsidies on firms. A sudden economy-wide one is a supply shock.
Anything other than the good's own price that changes supply and shifts the curve: input costs, technology, taxes and subsidies on producers, expectations and the number of sellers.
A direct (positive) relationship: two variables rise or fall together. In an inverse (negative) relationship, one rises as the other falls.

A person who wants a job but has stopped looking because they believe none is available. Discouraged workers are not in the labor force; underemployed workers have part-time jobs but want full-time ones.
Any price at which quantity demanded and quantity supplied are not equal, so there is a shortage or a surplus and the price tends to move.
terms.topicTitle: Market Equilibrium, Disequilibrium, and Changes in Equilibrium

terms.def: Household income after taxes are paid and transfers received: what households can spend or save.
A sustained increase in an economy's potential output and real GDP per capita over many years, shown by the PPC shifting out and LRAS shifting right.
The way a society answers what to produce, how and for whom. A market economy leaves it to buyers and sellers, a command economy to government planners, and a mixed economy combines the two.
The price of one currency in units of another, such as 1.25 dollars per euro. The same rate written the other way is its reciprocal: 0.80 euro per dollar.

terms.term: exchange rate effect on net exports
terms.def: How a change in a currency's value changes net exports. Appreciation makes exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper at home, so net exports and AD fall; depreciation raises net exports and AD, other things equal.
terms.topicTitle: Changes in the Foreign Exchange Market and Net Exports
aka: net exports and the exchange rate

terms.def: The inflation rate households and firms expect, which they build into wages and prices. A rise in expected inflation shifts the SRPC right; the SRPC crosses LRPC at the expected rate.

Measuring GDP by adding spending on final goods and services: consumption + investment + government purchases + net exports, or <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C + I + G + (X - M)</annotation></semantics></math>.

Exports are goods and services produced at home and sold abroad; imports are produced abroad and bought at home. Net exports are <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X - M</annotation></semantics></math>.
The resources used to make goods and services: land (natural resources), labor (human effort), capital (tools, machines and buildings) and entrepreneurship (organizing production and taking risks).
Goods and services bought by their final users. Intermediate goods are used up to make other goods and are left out of GDP; value added is a firm's sales minus what it paid for intermediate goods.

A claim on money or future income, such as money, a bond or a share of stock. Bonds are loans to the issuer; stocks are shares of ownership. Liquidity is how easily an asset becomes money without losing value.

Changes in government purchases, taxes and transfer payments meant to shift aggregate demand. Expansionary fiscal policy raises AD; contractionary fiscal policy lowers it. Discretionary policy is a deliberate decision.

An income set in dollars that does not rise with prices, such as a pension that pays the same amount each month. Unanticipated inflation hurts people on fixed incomes and lenders and helps fixed-rate borrowers.

The market where currencies are bought and sold. In the market for one currency, demand comes from people abroad buying the country's goods, services and assets, supply comes from its residents buying foreign ones, and the equilibrium price is the exchange rate.
A banking system in which banks keep only part of their deposits as reserves (vault cash and deposits at the central bank) and lend out the rest.
terms.topicTitle: Banking and the Expansion of the Money Supply

terms.def: Unemployment while people search between jobs or enter the labor force, such as a nurse who moved and is applying for nursing jobs.
The extra goods both sides get when they specialize by comparative advantage and trade, letting each consume beyond its own production possibilities.
terms.topicTitle: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade

terms.def: A price index for all final goods and services produced in a country: nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100. It is 100 in the base year.
GDP divided by population: output per person, the usual measure for comparing material living standards across countries or over time.
Goods are physical items people value, such as bread or a car; services are actions done for someone, such as a haircut or a lesson.
Gross domestic product: the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given year.
The percent change in real GDP from one period to the next: (new minus old) divided by old, times 100.
The skills, knowledge, training and health that make workers more productive. Physical capital is the equipment, buildings and machines they work with; productivity is output per worker or per hour.

Increasing opportunity cost: each extra unit of a good costs more of the other good than the last, because resources are not equally suited to both; it bows the PPC outward. A straight PPC shows constant opportunity cost.
terms.topicTitle: Opportunity Cost and the Production Possibilities Curve (PPC)

terms.def: When demand and supply both shift, the change in either price or quantity that cannot be known without the sizes of the shifts.
terms.topicTitle: Market Equilibrium, Disequilibrium, and Changes in Equilibrium

terms.def: A rise in prices in general across the economy. The inflation rate is the percent change in a price index from one period to the next.
The price of borrowing: what a borrower pays each year for the use of money, as a percent of the amount borrowed. To a lender it is the reward for lending.

Movements of financial capital between countries as savers buy and sell assets abroad. Financial capital tends to flow toward the country with the higher real interest rate; an inflow is a capital and financial account credit and raises demand for the currency.
terms.topicTitle: Real Interest Rates and International Capital Flows

terms.def: The point where two curves cross. On a market graph it gives the one price at which the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer.
Everyone who is employed or unemployed. The labor force participation rate is the labor force divided by the adult population, times 100.
As the price of a good rises, the quantity buyers want falls, other things equal; the demand curve slopes downward.
As the price of a good rises, the quantity sellers offer rises, other things equal; the supply curve slopes upward.

A framework in which banks hold few reserves beyond what is required, so the central bank changes interest rates by changing reserves and the money supply: open market operations (buying or selling bonds), the discount rate and the reserve requirement.
The short run is the period in which nominal wages and some prices are fixed; the long run is long enough for all wages and prices to adjust.
Long-run aggregate supply: the real output an economy produces when wages and prices have fully adjusted, which is full-employment output. The LRAS curve is vertical at that output.
The idea that in the long run a change in the money supply changes only nominal variables, such as the price level and nominal GDP, and not real output, unemployment or the real interest rate.
The long-run Phillips curve: a vertical line at the natural rate of unemployment, showing that in the long run unemployment returns to the natural rate whatever the inflation rate.
The economy's return to full employment with no policy: in a recessionary gap nominal wages and input prices fall and SRAS shifts right; in an inflationary gap they rise and SRAS shifts left.
M1 is the most spendable money: currency held by the public, checkable deposits and other deposits that can be withdrawn at once. M2 is M1 plus small time deposits and retail money market funds.
terms.topicTitle: Definition, Measurement, and Functions of Money

terms.def: Marginal propensity to consume: the share of an extra dollar of disposable income that households spend, the change in consumption divided by the change in disposable income.
Marginal propensity to save: the share of an extra dollar of disposable income that households save. MPS = 1 - MPC.
Market equilibrium: the price and quantity at which the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied, where the demand and supply curves cross.
terms.topicTitle: Market Equilibrium, Disequilibrium, and Changes in Equilibrium

terms.def: The costs to firms of changing prices often, such as reprinting menus and updating price tags. Shoe-leather costs are the time and effort people spend holding less cash when inflation erodes its value.

Actions by the central bank to change interest rates and so shift aggregate demand. Expansionary policy lowers rates to fight a recessionary gap; contractionary policy raises them to fight an inflationary gap.
Anything widely accepted in payment for goods and services. Its three functions are a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value.
terms.topicTitle: Definition, Measurement, and Functions of Money

terms.def: Banks create money when they lend excess reserves, because each loan becomes a new deposit; as loans are spent and redeposited, the money supply expands by a multiple.
terms.topicTitle: Banking and the Expansion of the Money Supply

terms.def: How much money people want to hold at each nominal interest rate. It slopes down because the interest rate is the cost of holding money (asset demand), and it rises with the price level and real GDP (transaction demand).
The market where the demand for money meets the money supply. Its graph has the nominal interest rate on the vertical axis and the quantity of money on the horizontal axis.
The most the money supply can grow for each dollar of new excess reserves: 1 divided by the required reserve ratio. With a ratio of 0.1 it is 10.
terms.topicTitle: Banking and the Expansion of the Money Supply

terms.def: The total amount of money in an economy, usually measured by M1. Banks expand it when they lend, and the central bank influences it.
terms.topicTitle: Banking and the Expansion of the Money Supply

terms.def: A move from one point to another on the same curve, caused by a change in a variable on one of the graph's axes, such as the price of the good.
terms.topicTitle: Shifts Versus Movements Along a Curve

terms.def: The total amount a government owes at a point in time: the sum of its past deficits minus its past surpluses, owed to holders of its bonds.
terms.topicTitle: Government Deficits and the National Debt

terms.def: The unemployment rate when cyclical unemployment is zero: frictional plus structural unemployment. When the actual rate equals it, the economy is at full employment.
GDP measured at the prices of the year the output is produced, so it rises when prices rise even if output does not.
The interest rate stated on a loan or bond, in dollars, before any adjustment for inflation.
Production not sold in a market, such as cooking for your own family or volunteer work. The underground (informal) economy is market activity that goes unreported. Both are missing from measured GDP.
The value of the next-best alternative given up when you make a choice. Per unit, it is the amount of the other good given up divided by the amount gained.
terms.topicTitle: Opportunity Cost and the Production Possibilities Curve (PPC)

terms.def: Real GDP minus potential output. A negative (recessionary) gap means output is below potential and there is cyclical unemployment; a positive (inflationary) gap means output is above potential.

Two ways to read trade data. Output data give units made per worker (the cost of one good is the other good's output divided by its own); input data give hours per unit (the cost of one good is its own hours divided by the other good's hours).
terms.topicTitle: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade

terms.def: Fiscal and monetary policy used at the same time. When both push AD the same way the AD effect is clear but the interest rate effect may not be; when they push opposite ways the AD effect is indeterminate.
terms.topicTitle: Fiscal and Monetary Policy Actions in the Short Run

terms.def: The interest rate a central bank targets; for the Federal Reserve it is the federal funds rate, what banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves. With ample reserves it is set by administered rates such as the interest on reserve balances (IORB).
The real GDP an economy produces when unemployment is at its natural rate: full-employment output. It grows over time.
An outward shift of the whole PPC, caused by more resources or better technology, so the economy can make more of both goods. A loss of resources shifts it inward.
terms.topicTitle: Opportunity Cost and the Production Possibilities Curve (PPC)

terms.def: A number that compares the cost of a fixed market basket of goods in one year with its cost in a base year, where the index equals 100.
The average level of prices of all goods and services in the economy, measured by a price index such as the GDP deflator. It is the vertical axis of the aggregate demand graph.
The production possibilities curve: a graph of every combination of two goods an economy can make when it uses all its resources and technology efficiently.
terms.topicTitle: Opportunity Cost and the Production Possibilities Curve (PPC)

terms.def: Productive efficiency: making the most output possible with the resources available, shown by a point on the PPC. A point inside the curve is inefficient, with resources idle or misused.
terms.topicTitle: Opportunity Cost and the Production Possibilities Curve (PPC)

terms.def: The amount of a good buyers want at one particular price. A change in the good's own price changes the quantity demanded, a movement along the demand curve.
The amount of a good sellers offer at one particular price. A change in the good's own price changes the quantity supplied, a movement along the supply curve.

The theory built on the equation of exchange, M x V = P x Y: if velocity and real output are steady, the price level moves in proportion to the money supply, so in the long run faster money growth means higher inflation.
aka: M x V = P x Y

terms.def: GDP measured at base-year prices, so it changes only when the quantity of goods and services produced changes. Real GDP = nominal GDP divided by the GDP deflator, times 100.
The interest rate adjusted for inflation: the nominal interest rate minus the expected inflation rate. It measures the gain in buying power a lender earns and the true cost of borrowing.
A nominal value (in dollars of the day) adjusted for prices: nominal value divided by a price index, times 100. A real wage is what a nominal wage buys in base-year dollars.
The reserves a bank must hold: its deposits times the required reserve ratio. Excess reserves are any reserves above that amount, which the bank can lend.
terms.topicTitle: Banking and the Expansion of the Money Supply

terms.def: The basic economic problem: people's wants are greater than the limited resources available to satisfy them, so choices must be made.
The whole curve moving to a new position because something other than the graphed variables changed; right means a larger quantity at every price, left a smaller one.
terms.topicTitle: Shifts Versus Movements Along a Curve

terms.def: Short-run aggregate supply: the total real output firms supply at each price level while nominal wages and some prices are fixed. The SRAS curve slopes up.
The short-run Phillips curve: a downward-sloping curve showing the short-run trade-off between the inflation rate and the unemployment rate. A change in AD moves the economy along it.
At a price below equilibrium, the amount by which quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied (Qd minus Qs). A shortage pushes the price up.
terms.topicTitle: Market Equilibrium, Disequilibrium, and Changes in Equilibrium

terms.def: How steep a line is: the change in the vertical value divided by the change in the horizontal value between two points (rise over run).
Concentrating production on the goods a person or country makes at the lowest opportunity cost, and trading for the rest.
terms.topicTitle: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade

terms.def: How many dollars real GDP changes for each dollar of new spending, 1 / MPS, because each round of spending is partly re-spent (the multiplier effect).
Nominal wages (and some prices) that do not adjust right away when the price level changes, often because of contracts. They make SRAS slope up.
Unemployment when workers' skills or locations do not match the jobs available, often after technology or the pattern of demand changes.
The overstatement of inflation by a fixed-basket index when people switch from goods whose prices rose to cheaper substitutes.
The two reasons demand slopes down: a lower price makes the good cheaper than its alternatives (substitution effect) and raises what buyers' incomes can buy (income effect).
At a price above equilibrium, the amount by which quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded (Qs minus Qd). A surplus pushes the price down.
terms.topicTitle: Market Equilibrium, Disequilibrium, and Changes in Equilibrium

terms.def: How many dollars real GDP changes for each dollar of tax change, -MPC / MPS. It is negative and one smaller in size than the spending multiplier.
The rate at which one good is exchanged for another in trade, such as 1 hat for 2.5 shirts. Both sides gain when it lies between their two opportunity costs.
terms.topicTitle: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade

terms.def: Giving up some of one thing to get more of another. Because resources are scarce, every choice involves a trade-off.
Money the government pays to households without buying a good or service in return, such as pensions or unemployment benefits. Transfers are not part of G; they raise disposable income.

Inflation different from what people anticipated when they signed loans, wage contracts or pensions. Unanticipated inflation redistributes purchasing power; anticipated inflation is built into those agreements.
A combination on or inside the PPC is attainable with today's resources and technology; a combination outside it is unattainable until the curve shifts outward.
terms.topicTitle: Opportunity Cost and the Production Possibilities Curve (PPC)

terms.def: The percent of the labor force that is unemployed: unemployed divided by labor force, times 100. A person is unemployed if they have no job, are available and looked for work recently.

An upward-sloping curve rises to the right (positive slope); a downward-sloping curve falls to the right (negative slope). A vertical line keeps the horizontal value fixed; a horizontal line keeps the vertical value fixed.
The average number of times a dollar is spent on final goods and services in a year: nominal GDP divided by the money supply.
The real wealth effect: a lower price level raises what savings can buy, so consumption rises. With the interest rate effect and the exchange rate effect, it explains why AD slopes down.
